issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction in the present matter.

facts: The Juvenile Justice Board passed an order on 12.04.2022 to conduct an inquiry, which the Supreme Court found to be legally invalid ("non-est") under Section 7(4) of the Act.
The Board later dismissed an application to terminate these proceedings, and this dismissal was challenged in the High Court through a revision petition.
The revision petition filed in the High Court incorrectly cited Sections 397/399 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.).
law: Section 102 of the relevant Act grants the High Court revisional powers over any order or proceeding from the Juvenile Justice Board or Children's Court.
This revisional power allows the High Court to satisfy itself as to the legality or propriety of an order and has no prescribed time limit for filing.
Under Section 7(4) of the Act, the proceedings before the Board should not have continued after a prior order dated 05.04.2022.
application: The Supreme Court held that the incorrect citation of the Cr.P.C. sections in the revision petition was a minor error, as the High Court inherently possessed the power to review the matter under Section 102 of the Act.
The Court found that the High Court was justified in exercising its revisional power not just on the legality but also on the "propriety" of the Board's proceedings.
The Board's decision to continue the inquiry via its order dated 12.04.2022 was contrary to Section 7(4) and therefore legally invalid ("non-est").

Because the Board's proceedings were improper and its order was void, the High Court's intervention through its revisional jurisdiction was deemed maintainable and correct, even though the invalid order was not challenged through a separate appeal.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court did not err in exercising its revisional jurisdiction. The High Court correctly used its powers under Section 102 of the Act to intervene in the legally improper proceedings of the Board, and the procedural mistake of citing the wrong law in the petition did not invalidate this exercise of power.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in its order dealing with the procedure under Section 7(4) of the Act, specifically regarding the prevalence of the Principal Magistrate's opinion when a dissenting view is recorded by another member of the Board without reasons.

facts: The Juvenile Justice Board (the Board), consisting of the Principal Magistrate and one other member, heard arguments on whether a Child in Conflict with Law (CCL) should be tried by the Children's Court.
On April 5, 2022, the Principal Magistrate recorded his opinion that the CCL should be tried by the Children's Court.
The other member of the Board recorded a dissenting view but did not provide any reasons at that time.
The High Court, in a revision petition, held that the Principal Magistrate's order from April 5, 2022, was final.
law: Section 7(4) of the Juvenile Justice Act provides the procedure for decisions by the Board when there is a difference of opinion.
The law states that the opinion of the majority shall prevail.
However, if there is no majority, the opinion of the Principal Magistrate shall prevail.
application: The Supreme Court analyzed the situation on April 5, 2022. The Board consisted of only two members: the Principal Magistrate and another member.
Since the two members disagreed, there was no majority opinion possible.
The Court applied the specific provision of Section 7(4) which dictates that in the absence of a majority, the Principal Magistrate's opinion is decisive.
The Court noted that the other member's dissent was recorded without any reasons, which further solidified the finality of the Principal Magistrate's reasoned order.
Therefore, the order signed by the Principal Magistrate on April 5, 2022, was final and conclusive. Any subsequent proceedings by the Board on that issue were deemed invalid and without jurisdiction.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court did not err in its order. It affirmed that under Section 7(4) of the Act, when the Board has only two members who disagree, the opinion of the Principal Magistrate prevails, making their order final. The challenge to the High Court's decision was therefore rejected.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction in the present matter.
appellant_arguments: The Board's order to transfer the case to the Children's Court was invalid because it was passed after the statutory three-month period had expired, rendering any subsequent action non-est.
The proper legal remedy against the Board's order was an appeal to the Court of Sessions, not a revision petition before the High Court.
respondent_arguments: All possible arguments had already been raised by the appellant and were considered by the High Court in the revision petition.
Allowing the appellant to challenge the order again before a lower authority would be a futile exercise and would only cause further delays in the process.

cases.case_name: Topline Shoes Ltd. v. Corporation Bank
cases.principle: Relied on for the principle that procedural time limits can be interpreted as directory rather than mandatory to serve the interests of justice.

Merely because a provision of law is couched in a negative language implying mandatory character, it is not without exceptions and may be held to be directory, keeping in view the entire context in which the provision was enacted.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: While courts generally cannot add words to a statute that are not there (causus omissus), it is permissible to supply words by implication which appear to have been accidentally omitted if the only alternative is to adopt a construction that deprives the existing words of the statute of all meaning.
obiter: The use of the word 'shall' in a statute does not necessarily mean it is mandatory in every case; the court may ascertain the real intention of the legislature by examining the entire scope of the statute.

Even if a provision is framed in negative language implying a mandatory character, courts may interpret it as directory after considering the context and the legislative scheme, especially where consequences for non-compliance are not specified.
The principle of literal construction of a statute, without examining its context and scheme, may not serve the purpose of the statute.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court found no error in the High Court's decision to exercise its revisional jurisdiction, concluding that the High Court's order was correct and did not require interference. The Court also acknowledged procedural anomalies in the Juvenile Justice Act regarding dissenting opinions on the Board but determined these did not invalidate the proceedings in this specific case, though they should be addressed for future clarity.
legal_tests_applied: The court applied a test of statutory interpretation to determine if a provision is mandatory or directory, stating that the use of the word “shall” is not always mandatory and that the court must ascertain the real intention of the legislature by examining the context and entire scheme of the statute, rather than relying on literal construction alone.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's challenge to the High Court's use of revisional jurisdiction failed because the Supreme Court explicitly found that "There is no error in exercise of revisional jurisdiction by the High Court in the present matter."

The appellant's argument regarding the procedural flaw of an unreasoned dissenting opinion was not sufficient to invalidate the Board's order, as the Court, while acknowledging "anomalies" in the procedure that should be streamlined for the future, did not find the error to be fatal in this instance.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position was upheld because the Supreme Court directly affirmed the High Court's actions, stating there was no error in its exercise of revisional jurisdiction.

The respondent's argument that remanding the matter would be a futile exercise causing further delay was implicitly accepted by the Court's decision to dispose of the appeal without overturning the High Court's substantive findings on jurisdiction.
policy_considerations: The Court expressed a forward-looking policy concern to improve the legal process, noting that anomalies in the statutory procedure for Board decisions "should also be addressed, so as to streamline the procedure in future. We also think in the same direction, keeping in view the spirit of law."

The Court referenced the principle of balancing procedural timelines with substantive justice, noting that where a statute sets a time limit without providing for penal consequences, the focus should be on avoiding prolonged proceedings while also considering all facts and circumstances to prevent grave injustice.
